tldr: Headlines across all 12 buckets overwhelmingly frame the UK ATC outage as mass passenger disruption — 'chaos,' 'nightmare,' and scale figures (1,000–2,000 cancellations, 65,000+ passengers) dominate the global title layer; one in four headlines foreground a cyberattack suspicion despite its official denial; and UK domestic plus wire-service titles uniquely advance an accountability narrative demanding the NATS chief’s resignation or government summons.

single_outlet_findings.finding: Only headline simultaneously demanding the NATS boss resign AND linking the current outage to the 2023 failure — constructs a pattern of repeated institutional breakdown rather than an isolated glitch, amplifying accountability pressure at the title layer.

Only headline framing the outage as a passenger-rights question ('what are your rights if you have been affected?') — the sole consumer-entitlement angle across all 26 articles; inverts the agency from operator failure to reader recourse.

Only headline reporting that air traffic had already resumed ('ripreso traffico aereo') — the sole recovery/positive signal visible at title level, in contrast to the chaos and ongoing disruption framing across every other outlet.

Only headline naming a specific national carrier (Finnair) rather than UK airports or NATS — localizes the story as a Scandinavian aviation disruption, making the UK outage legible through its domestic knock-on impact.

bottom_line: The global headline layer sells the UK ATC failure as a consumer catastrophe — chaos language and mass-cancellation scale figures dominate — while the political reckoning (government summons, resignation demands) and the cyberattack suspicion are the secondary frames visible primarily to UK domestic and wire-service readers.
